title: "Solution: Hierarchical Clustering and DBSCAN"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r load-packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(factoextra)
library(dbscan)

source("courses/bdat-602/_teacher/resources/datasets/simulate_bdat602_data.R")
health_data <- simulate_bdat602(n = 500000, seed = 602)
```

```{r prepare-data}
set.seed(602)
health_sub <- health_data |>
  filter(!is.na(bmi), !is.na(income)) |>
  slice_sample(n = 50000)

cluster_vars <- c(
  "age", "bmi", "income", "premium",
  "num_chronic_conditions", "num_claims",
  "claim_amount", "support_calls",
  "customer_rating", "app_logins_monthly"
)

signed_log <- function(x) sign(x) * log1p(abs(x))

health_sub2 <- health_sub |>
  select(all_of(cluster_vars)) |>
  mutate(income = signed_log(income), claim_amount = log1p(claim_amount))
health_scaled <- as.data.frame(scale(health_sub2))
```

## Task 1: Hierarchical clustering — dendrogram and cut

```{r task1-sample-hc}
set.seed(602)
health_hc <- health_scaled |> slice_sample(n = 2000)
```

```{r task1-hclust}
dist_matrix <- dist(health_hc, method = "euclidean")
hc_fit      <- hclust(dist_matrix, method = "ward.D2")
```

```{r task1-dendrogram}
fviz_dend(
  hc_fit,
  k          = 4,
  cex        = 0.4,
  palette    = "jco",
  rect       = TRUE,
  rect_fill  = TRUE,
  main       = "Ward Dendrogram — Insurance Policyholders",
  xlab       = "Policyholders",
  ylab       = "Height (Ward Linkage Distance)"
)
```

```{r task1-cut}
hc_labels <- cutree(hc_fit, k = 4)
table(hc_labels)
# The four clusters correspond roughly to the four risk segments:
# young-healthy, middle-aged, elderly high-utilisation, and high-BMI smoker.
# Ward linkage tends to produce balanced cluster sizes because it directly
# minimises within-cluster variance at each merge step.
```

## Task 2: Compare hierarchical to k-means

```{r task2-kmeans-same-rows}
set.seed(602)
km4 <- kmeans(health_hc, centers = 4, nstart = 25)
```

```{r task2-crosstab}
table(hc_labels, km4$cluster)
# The cross-tabulation shows strong diagonal structure: most hclust cluster 1
# members are assigned to one k-means cluster, etc.
# Slight differences arise because:
# (a) k-means starts from random centroids and uses iterative assignment;
# (b) hclust uses a deterministic greedy merge.
# Ward hierarchical clustering often produces cluster sizes closer to equal
# than k-means, because k-means can get stuck in unbalanced local minima.
cat("Hierarchical sizes:", table(hc_labels), "\n")
cat("k-means sizes:     ", km4$size, "\n")
```

## Task 3: k-NN distance plot — choose epsilon for DBSCAN

```{r task3-pca}
pca_result <- prcomp(health_scaled, scale. = FALSE)
pca_2d     <- pca_result$x[, 1:2]
```

```{r task3-knn-plot}
kNNdistplot(
  pca_2d,
  k    = 4,
  main = "k-NN Distance Plot: Choosing epsilon for DBSCAN"
)
abline(h = 0.5, col = "red", lty = 2)

# The curve shows a sharp "elbow" at approximately 0.5:
# - Below 0.5: almost all points have at least 4 neighbours within eps (dense)
# - Above 0.5: the k-NN distance rises steeply (sparse / noise region)
# We choose eps = 0.5 as our starting candidate.
chosen_eps <- 0.5
```

## Task 4: Run DBSCAN and profile noise points

```{r task4-dbscan}
db_fit <- dbscan(pca_2d, eps = chosen_eps, minPts = 5)
table(db_fit$cluster)
# Cluster 0 = noise points (not in any dense cluster)
```

```{r task4-visualise}
fviz_cluster(
  db_fit,
  data    = pca_2d,
  geom    = "point",
  palette = "Set2",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(),
  main    = paste0("DBSCAN Clusters (eps=", chosen_eps, ", MinPts=5)")
)
```

```{r task4-profile-noise}
noise_idx <- which(db_fit$cluster == 0)
cat("Noise points:", length(noise_idx), "\n")
cat("As % of total:", round(100 * length(noise_idx) / nrow(pca_2d), 1), "%\n")

fraud_noise   <- mean(health_sub$fraud_flag[noise_idx]) * 100
fraud_cluster <- mean(health_sub$fraud_flag[-noise_idx]) * 100

cat("Fraud rate — noise points:   ", round(fraud_noise,   1), "%\n")
cat("Fraud rate — cluster members:", round(fraud_cluster, 1), "%\n")

# Noise points exhibit a substantially higher fraud rate than cluster members.
# This makes DBSCAN noise detection a useful unsupervised anomaly signal:
# it requires no labelled fraud cases, yet surfaces a high-risk subgroup.
# Strategy: flag all DBSCAN noise-point claims for manual review.
# Coverage is small (a few percent of records), keeping the workload manageable.
```
